lecture19.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate
teaching: A **single neuron** multiplies its inputs by weights and adds the products into one number. A **neural network** combines these operations into layers, turning one input vector into a decision vector.

An **LLM** processes fifteen vectors through successive layers and predicts a sixteenth vector, a probability distribution over the next token. An **agentic system** joins whole LLMs into a graph that outlines, writes, criticizes, revises and finalizes the response.
The critic and reviser form a loop so a revised draft can be evaluated again. The agents communicate in English and can work in other human languages and computer languages.
**Inference uses inner products**, while learning uses **SGD and dynamic programming**. Inference processes current inputs with learned weights, while learning changes the weights to reduce error.

The agents communicate through **language**. One model’s written output becomes information another model can use, so the graph coordinates whole language models rather than individual neurons. The agents can speak to each other in English, while the models can also work in other human languages and computer languages.

**Inference uses inner products, and learning uses SGD with dynamic programming.** Inference processes the current inputs with the learned weights. **Stochastic gradient descent**, or SGD, changes weights to reduce prediction error, while backpropagation uses **dynamic programming** to organize the backward calculation. These operations support the small network as well as the language models joined into the agentic graph.

**A neural network makes one static decision, but real cognition flows in time.** A network is given an input, such as the pixels of a face or a spoken vowel, and it makes one decision about it. Language and speech keep changing from moment to moment, so one static decision cannot capture them. Take the sentence “The wolves that run around Catalina Island ___.” A speaker of English fills the gap with “are,” because the verb agrees with “wolves” however many words come between them. Real language skill depends on these long-distance relationships. Speech has them too. A listener can tell that a sentence is about to end because the speaker slows down, so the timing far back in the sentence is related to how it ends. The **sigmoid** carries two ideas. A neuron is either on or off, and people sort things into categories, treating two physically different things as the same and two very similar things as different.

**An agentic system gives each LLM a different job, and the LLMs check each other.** The first LLM is told not to answer the question and to write an outline. The second writes a first draft from the outline. The third criticizes the draft, looking for spelling errors, grammar errors and flaws, and it can search the web to check that a reference exists. The draft goes back and forth between the critic and the writer, usually up to a limit of 3 or 4 rounds. A final LLM then writes the answer the user sees, which is why an answer can take a minute or two. A **hallucination** is an answer that sounds right but is made up, such as a legal reference that does not exist. Hallucination dropped enormously once LLMs were set up to check each other, although it has not disappeared. The systems have also grown. The neural networks studied so far have thousands of W’s, the earliest LLMs had hundreds of millions, and the largest current systems are thought to have trillions.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers
teaching: **Predicting the next word is difficult**, so an LLM uses many layers to develop its input representations. Each layer transforms the vectors produced by the preceding layer.

Within a layer, **heads work in parallel as different experts**. Their contributions are combined into new representations, and the next layer repeats the process with those representations. Heads contribute within one stage, while layers provide successive stages.

**The next layer repeats the process with the representations it receives.** It has parallel heads whose contributions are combined again. The model therefore develops its representations through a succession of layers, rather than making its final prediction directly from the original input vectors.

**Heads and layers add different kinds of structure.** Heads provide parallel contributions within one processing stage, while layers provide successive stages that refine the vectors further. The prediction at the end depends on these contributions being combined within stages and developed across stages.

**Each head is its own neural network that makes a decision, and each layer has its own set of heads.** Imagine wanting to improve yourself and visiting five classes. In the first class, each student gives advice, and each student is a head. The advice from all the students is combined, which gives a better representation of each vector. The second class is the next layer, with its own heads, and the same thing happens again. This continues until the representations of the vectors are good enough to predict the next word.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth
teaching: A **dynamical system** applies a rule to its state and feeds the resulting state back in. In the oscillator, position is updated using the old velocity, then velocity is updated using that new position. Repeating the rule produces oscillation.

In **Jordan’s recurrent network**, plan and state units feed a hidden layer, output returns to state units, and self-connections preserve a fading trace. The weights are reused over time, so recent outputs affect the next output.

An **LLM** transforms vectors through successive layers, so depth plays the role of time. Following one number through the layers gives a changing curve. Each layer has its own weights, unlike the same rule reused across time in the oscillator and recurrent network.
The small stock-return graph traces Small, Medium and Large series fluctuating over the same period, another example of quantities changing over time.

**In the LLM comparison, depth plays the role of time.** Fifteen vectors enter the first layer and are transformed by its weights. The resulting vectors enter the next layer, where another transformation takes place. Following one number upward through the layers gives a sequence of changing values, which can be drawn as a curve even though it is not the oscillator’s cosine.

**The rules are organized differently in these systems.** The oscillator and Jordan network apply the same rule repeatedly as time advances. The LLM uses a separate set of weights at each layer, so its successive transformations follow the depth of the network. What connects the examples is the dependence of each new state on the state produced just before it. The small stock-return graph traces Small, Medium and Large series over the same period. They fluctuate, rise and fall over the years, giving another example of quantities changing over time.

**An LLM is a dynamical system in the same sense as the oscillator.** In the oscillator, knowing x gives the next v, and knowing v gives the next x, so the two numbers keep recreating each other. An LLM does the same kind of thing with tens of thousands of numbers, many times over. Each layer takes the current vectors and produces new vectors. This is the idea that ties the physical systems and the AI systems of the course together.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences
teaching: An **LLM** receives fifteen vectors and predicts the following one. The vectors can represent words in a sentence, frames of a spectrogram, patches of a picture, or amino acids in the **insulin B chain**.

The picture is divided into sixteen patches, with fifteen given and the bottom-right patch left to predict. In the protein example the next residue is Y. The original materials differ, but all are represented as **sequences of vectors**.

The last example is a **protein, the insulin B chain**, read as **15 amino acids**, F V N Q H L C G S H L V E A L, drawn folding into a helix. Each amino acid is a vector, and **x₁₆ is the next residue**, which is **Y**. The same sixteenth slot sits at the end of every sequence.

The takeaway states the point of the four examples. **The LLM only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, pixels and molecules all become sequences of vectors, so **one machine asks one question, what is x₁₆?** Whatever the source, learning to predict the next vector in a sequence is the task the model is built for.

**The first LLMs worked on text, and they learned by having their W’s changed after every wrong guess.** Take “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ___.” A speaker of English expects “branch” or “mat,” and never “may,” “in” or “the.” An LLM starts with random W’s, so at first it predicts impossible words. After each guess the W’s change so that the prediction becomes more like the actual next word. This is repeated millions and billions of times, until the model has the same grasp of English that a speaker has.

**Within about two years, the same design was used for speech, images and proteins, only by changing what the vectors stand for.** For speech, each vector stands for a small piece of a spectrogram, and the model predicts the next piece. A spectrogram is a sequence of vectors in time, just as a sentence is. For an image, which does not vary in time, the image is cut into patch 1, patch 2, patch 3 and so on. Each patch is treated as if it were a word, and the model predicts patch 16. For a protein, the sequence is made of 20 kinds of amino acid. The sequence decides how the protein folds into its 3D shape, and the shape decides what the protein does in the body. Predicting an amino acid from the others is the same game, and this work received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The layers and heads stayed the same in every case. Speech synthesis from before LLMs could be understood but sounded unnatural, and the LLM systems sound natural.

**The same technology solving all of these problems supports the horizontal view of cognition.** A **verticalist** holds that vision, hearing and language are separate skills, each with its own part of the brain. The **horizontal** view, proposed by the neural network researchers of the 1980s, holds that the same computations are used in every skill. The brain areas for hearing and vision are in different places, but their cells are organized in the same way and have the same feedback loops. One design of layers with heads then solved language, speech, vision and protein folding.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?
teaching: One-syllable words like Don, mat and fish follow a **consonant, vowel, consonant** pattern. Clusters are allowed **before and after the vowel** only in certain orders, so split, flat, desk and help are words while *sblit, *lfat, *desb and *hepl are impossible, with the order mirroring around the vowel.

A **long word is a chain of syllables**, each obeying the same rules. t·l is fine across a break in At·lan·tic, but **tl cannot start a syllable**, so *tlantic is impossible, and ng can end a syllable but never start one.

The third row has **words of many syllables**, with dots marking syllable breaks, such as **ba·na·na, win·dow, pump·kin, nap·kin, At·lan·tic, ath·lete, ad·mit and spa·ghet·ti**. Atlantic, athlete and admit contain t followed by l, th followed by l, and d followed by m. Those pairs are fine inside the word because a syllable break falls between them, but they cannot begin a word, so *tlantic, *thlete and *dmit are impossible. Likewise ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but never start one, so *ngapkin is impossible.

The rule for the whole page is that **a long word is a chain of syllables**, and every syllable obeys the same rules. **t·l is fine across a break, but tl cannot start a syllable.** This is **phonotactic knowledge**, the knowledge of which sound sequences a language allows, and English speakers have it without ever being taught it.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge
teaching: Guessing the **next letter** of a word start shows **phonotactic knowledge**. After a vowel, as in **ra_**, almost anything can follow. At the start of a word the choices narrow, to **l, r or a vowel** after sp_, b_ and f_, and to **only a vowel** after skr_ and m_.

Each item also has an impossible continuation, such as *spn, *kt, *skrl or *mb. **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆**, so a **GPT** trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, with a broad distribution after ra_ and a sharply peaked one after skr_.

These guesses follow the rules for English syllables. What can follow a starting consonant is exactly what an English onset allows, and the impossible continuations are clusters that English never allows at the start of a syllable. Guessing well requires knowing English phonotactics.

The takeaway connects this to LLMs. **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆.** A **GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling**, because its predicted distribution has to match these patterns. After ra_ its distribution is spread broad over many letters, and after skr_ it is sharply peaked on a few vowels.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables
What an LLM learns
teaching: An LLM learns by guessing a **hidden word**. In “The chef cracks the,” each earlier word gives a clue about the last word, and these links are **interdependencies**. The model spreads its bets over “egg,” “nut” and “code,” with the largest bet on “egg.”
**Learning is nudging the weights** so the right word gets a bigger bet next time. The same idea holds when the signal contains words, sounds and images.

**Learning is nudging the weights so that these guesses get better.** A nudge is a small change to a weight. After the true word is revealed, the weights change a little, so the right word gets a bigger bet the next time.

**The same idea holds when the signal contains more than words.** The signal is the sequence the model reads. It can hold **words, sounds and images** together, and the model still guesses a hidden piece from the other pieces. The content of the signal changes, while the way the model learns stays the same.

**Guessing the next word is called the GPT task, and it is how these systems learn.** After “The chef cracks the,” there is a big probability for “egg,” smaller ones for “nut” and “code,” and hardly any chance of “the.” The weights are nudged by **backpropagation**, so the guesses get better and better. **Multimodal systems**, which handle text, speech and images together, are about two to three years old. People are multimodal too. A listener hears the speech, follows the words and watches the gestures, and combines all of them into one meaning.

sections.title: Text, speech and images in three different forms
teaching: Text is **already a row of pieces**, so each piece can become a vector. Speech is **air pressure changing in time**, and an image is **a grid of light**. Neither one contains words.
An LLM can only read a row of vectors. Speech and images therefore have to be **converted into rows of vectors** before the model can read them with text.
**An image is a grid of light.** Each position in the grid has its own brightness and colour. The image of an egg in a pan contains no words either, and its pieces are not arranged in a row.

**The first job is a conversion.** All three forms have to become rows of vectors, because a row of vectors is all the LLM can read. Once speech and images are rows too, one model can read them together with text.

**The three forms can be three versions of one message.** There are the words, there is the speech signal of someone saying “now crack the egg,” which is the pressure variation in front of the mouth, and there is an image of an egg that has been cracked. A multimodal agent understands how the sound, the words and the image relate. Before multimodal systems, each kind of model was trained by itself. A text model predicted “egg” from “now crack the.” A speech model had a small piece of the signal taken out and predicted the next piece. A vision model had a patch taken out and predicted the missing patch.

sections.title: Speech becomes a row of frame vectors
teaching: Speech is cut into short slices called **frames**, each about 20 milliseconds long. A **speech encoder**, a network trained on a large amount of audio, turns each slice into a vector.
One second of speech becomes **50 vectors in time order**. The speech is then a row, just like a sentence.

**One second of speech becomes 50 vectors.** Each slice lasts about 20 milliseconds, and 50 slices of that length fill one second. The vectors stay in time order, so the earliest slice comes first in the row.
**Speech is now a row, just like a sentence.** A sentence is a row of word vectors, and the sliced speech is a row of frame vectors. The LLM reads both the same way, one vector after another.

sections.title: Images become a row of patch vectors
teaching: An image is cut into small squares called **patches**. The 16 patches of the egg image are laid out in a row in reading order, so the image becomes a sequence.
A **vision encoder** gives one vector per patch. Real systems use patches of 14 to 16 pixels, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.
**One vector comes out for each patch.** The 16 patches give 16 vectors, and the vectors keep the order of the patches. The image has become a row that the LLM can read.
**Real systems use much smaller patches.** The 4 by 4 grid keeps the example simple. Real systems use patches of 14 to 16 pixels, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.

sections.title: One row with three senses
teaching: Image patches, speech frames and words go into **one row**, with the last word hidden. The earlier words still give clues about the hidden word.
A patch containing an egg and the sound of cracking also help. These links between senses are **cross-modal dependencies**. The game is the same, and some clues now come from other senses.
**The game is exactly the same as before.** The model guesses the hidden piece from the pieces it can read. It then learns from how good the guess was.

**The source of the clues is what changes.** With text alone, every clue is a word. In the combined row, a clue can also be an image patch or a speech frame, so the model has more information for the same guess.

**The game played inside one modality can be played across modalities, because the same technology is used for all three.** The patches of an image are followed, in the same sequence, by the frames of speech, and then by the text vectors. The model is asked to predict the next word from all of these vectors, not only from the words before it. A system trained this way has many more W’s. Its W’s are no longer only about text, only about speech or only about vision. They are about how the image patches of an egg relate to the speech vectors of someone talking about eggs, and how both relate to the words. After training over and over on a great deal of speech, images and words, the W’s become truly multimodal. The system then knows the relationship between spoken language, written language and what is seen. It is still built from layers with heads, and from W’s doing inner products and sigmoids.

sections.title: Three cute puppies as an image, speech and words
teaching: “Three cute puppies” is given as an image cut into **18 patches**, as a **spectrogram** of the spoken phrase, and as three written words. In the spectrogram, time runs left to right, higher means higher frequency and darker means more energy.
These are **three views of one event**. Training puts all three into one row and hides one piece for the model to guess.

**Each word occupies its own stretch of time.** “Three” comes first, “cute” comes second and “puppies” comes last. Each thin column of the spectrogram is one frame. The speech was made with a speech synthesizer, an MBROLA diphone voice.

**The image, the sound and the words are three views of one event.** In training, all three go into one row. The model then plays the same game on that row, in which one piece is hidden and the model guesses it.

**The example comes from ordinary social media data.** Someone posts an image of three cute puppies, writes “three cute puppies” under it, and adds a video in which they say the same words. The same event is now present in all three modalities, so a system has something to train on. The W’s of these systems come from data like this, which people produced. For that reason some lawmakers argue that people should be paid for the data the systems were trained on, and this is being argued in court.

sections.title: Training example 1 predicts the next word
teaching: The row holds the image, the sound and the words “three cute,” and the last word is hidden. With the words alone, the bets are spread over “kittens,” “puppies” and “babies.”
With the image and the sound, the bet piles up on **“puppies.”** The model bet 0.85 on the true word, so the error is small and **the nudge to the weights is small**.
**The true word is then revealed, and the model is graded.** The grade depends on how much the model bet on the true word. The true word is “puppies,” and the model bet 0.85 on it.
**A large bet on the truth gives a small nudge.** The model bet a lot on the true word, so the error is small. Because the error is small, the weights move only a little.

**The same post can train the system in three separate ways, and the first way hides a word.** The system is given a few of the words, such as “three cute,” together with all of the speech frames and all of the image patches. It has to predict the next text word, and its W’s change so that it predicts that word better.

sections.title: Training example 2 predicts a sound frame
teaching: The hidden piece is a **sound frame**, and the row holds the image, the words and the sound heard so far. The earlier frames help because the voice and the formants change smoothly. The words say the next sound is the vowel in “pup,” and the image backs up the words.
A frame is a column of numbers giving the energy in each frequency band. The guess is close but not exact, and **the error nudges the weights**.

**A frame is a column of numbers.** Each number is how much energy there is in one frequency band, and 16 bands are displayed. The model’s guess is close to the true frame but not exact. The error is how far apart each number in the guess is from the matching number in the truth.
**That error nudges the weights.** The weights change so that the next guess for a frame is closer. Some systems predict a code for each frame instead of the raw numbers.

**The second way hides part of the speech.** The system is given the patches of the image, the words, and half of the speech. It has to predict the next bit of speech, and it uses the speech frames, the text words and the image patches to do it.

sections.title: Training example 3 predicts an image patch
teaching: The hidden piece is an **image patch**, and the row holds the words, the sound and the patches drawn so far. The earlier patches give background and two puppies. “Three” says one more puppy must appear, and “puppies” says to expect dog ears.
The guess is a blurry ear in the average colour of the first two puppies, while the true puppy is dark. **The biggest error is the colour**, because no clue said the third puppy is dark.

**The guess is a blurry puppy ear in the average colour of the first two puppies.** The true patch belongs to a dark puppy. The biggest error is therefore the colour, because nothing in the words, the sound or the earlier patches said the third puppy would be dark.
**That error nudges the weights.** Only systems that also produce images are trained this way. Systems that only read images usually skip this step.

**The third way hides a patch, and the words and the speech are what make the right guess likely.** The system is given the words, all of the speech, and some of the patches. The next patch is the third dog. From two dogs in the image alone, the next patch could be a kennel, a person or the sun in the background. But the text contains “three” and “puppies,” and the speech says “three puppies.” So the probability of a person, a house or a kennel is very low, and the highest probability is that a third puppy is there. The other modalities spell out what is in the image.

sections.title: Every piece can be the hidden one
teaching: A hidden word, a hidden frame or a hidden patch each receives clues from the words, the sound and the image. For a hidden word, “three cute” calls for a plural noun, the word was just spoken, and the image contains puppies.
A clue from **the same sense** says how the signal continues. Clues from **the other senses** say what the thing is. Each sense fills gaps the others leave.

**For a hidden patch, the image itself says how the patch should continue.** The fur and the background carry on from the earlier patches. The word “three” says one more puppy is coming, and the sound gives the same words in heard form.

**Clues from the same sense and clues from other senses do different jobs.** A clue from the same sense mostly says how the signal continues, as with grammar, smooth formants, and fur and background. Clues from the other senses mostly say what the thing is, which here is puppies, three of them. Training on all three senses together helps because each sense fills gaps the others leave.

**One situation can train the system in every direction.** The same post is used to go from speech and vision to text, from text and vision to speech, and through all the other possibilities. This is repeated over many different posts, such as three factories with people standing in front of them. **W’s are knowledge.** After this training, the knowledge in the W’s is about the bond between several skills, which are speaking, hearing and seeing. The idea behind each step is simple. Someone who understood the text system replaced the words with frames of speech, or with patches of an image.

sections.title: Talking back, and what is new
teaching: To speak, sound is compressed into **discrete codes** that work like new words in the vocabulary. The model predicts the next code like the next word, and a **decoder** turns the codes back into sound.

Three things are new, which are a shared currency of vectors in one row, data where the senses appear together, and a schedule that protects what was already learned. What stays the same is **finding the dependencies in the signal**.

**Three things are new.** The first is a shared currency, in which everything becomes vectors in one row. The second is data where the senses appear together. The third is a schedule that protects what was already learned.
**The learning rule stays the same.** The model still finds the dependencies in the signal. The signal has become wider, because it now holds words, sounds and images.

**A modality is like a sense, and language counts as one too.** At first there were LLMs for language alone, then for speech alone, for vision alone and for biology alone. Over the last three or four years, systems have intertwined all of them, and there are now agentic multimodal systems whose LLMs specialize in different things and talk to each other. **Biomedical multimodal LLMs** combine medical images such as MRI and ultrasound, the doctor’s notes, lab results and DNA or protein sequences in one system. Radiology was one of the first fields to change, and these systems have found tumors that doctors missed. They also make mistakes, as doctors do. An ordinary chat system already works this way. Asked a question in Armenian, it answered in Armenian, because its W’s know about a hundred languages, and it also takes images and speech. These systems need so many W’s partly because their knowledge is far wider than one person’s, covering about a thousand topics and a hundred languages.
